section_summary: This section concludes a nationwide 1948 newspaper directory, listing regional newspapers, personnel, circulation, facilities, affiliations, an index, and a newspaper-readership chart. It then contains a sequence of U.S. Political Adviser despatches summarizing Japanese press reactions from February through March 1949, including duplicated information copies and an enclosed interview with General Douglas MacArthur. Major subjects include the Yoshida cabinet, economic stabilization and budget policy, labor-law revision, Japanese neutrality and security, government-property sales, and proposals for an un-Japanese activities committee.

subfiles.title: Newspaper Directory: regional listings, index, and newspaper readers chart
subfiles.about: Concludes a national directory of Japanese newspapers with regional publication data, personnel, facilities, affiliations, an index, and readership statistics.
subfiles.summary: The directory entries cover newspapers in the San'in, Shikoku, Hokkaido, and Kyushu districts, giving addresses, circulation, advertising rates, publishers, senior editorial and business staff, branch offices, news-agency affiliations, equipment, and employment totals. Pages 183-184 supply an index of member dailies and a chart reporting total circulation, population, households, and major broadcasting locations as of April 1, 1948.

subfiles.title: Japanese Newspaper Reactions for Week Ending February 10, 1949 (Despatch No. 88)
subfiles.from: W. J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Summarizes Japanese press reaction to international diplomacy, labor policy, cabinet formation, crop prospects, and proposed repeal of American racial restrictions.
subfiles.summary: Tokyo editorials generally approved Acheson's insistence that any Stalin peace initiative proceed through the United Nations and debated statements made during Secretary Royall's visit, especially Gibson's comments on unions and strikes. Newspapers urged Yoshida to form a fresh, scandal-free one-party cabinet and discussed purge appeals. They also examined abnormal winter weather, grain and rice supplies, and a Judd bill removing legal barriers to Asian immigration and naturalization.

subfiles.title: Japanese Newspaper Reactions for the Week Ending February 17, 1949 (Despatch No. 108)
subfiles.from: W. J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese press discussion of Japan's strategic position and the creation of Yoshida's third cabinet.
subfiles.summary: The press gave leading attention to formation of the third Yoshida cabinet, while the Sorge case briefly dominated news coverage. Editorials questioned Japan's dependence on foreign powers for security and considered neutrality and peaceful reconstruction. Major papers criticized Yoshida's personal dominance, assessed the failed coalition maneuver with the Democratic Party, and weighed the cabinet's ability to implement the nine-point economic stabilization program.

subfiles.title: Japanese Newspaper Reactions for Week Ending February 24, 1949 (Despatch No. 122)
subfiles.from: Cloyce K. Huston, Counselor of Mission, for the Acting Political Adviser
subfiles.about: Summarizes Japanese editorials on American policy, self-reliance, labor-law revision, the national budget, and a proposed un-Japanese activities committee.
subfiles.summary: Newspapers responded to reassurances from Truman and Acheson by praising constructive Occupation policy while arguing that Japan must become more self-reliant. They debated revision of labor laws and treated the 1949-1950 budget as a central test of economic stabilization, focusing on taxation, prices, railway deficits, payroll reductions, and subsidies. Several editorials warned that an un-Japanese activities committee could revive ideological policing unless placed under firm constitutional and representative safeguards.

subfiles.title: Information Copy of Japanese Newspaper Reactions for Week Ending February 24, 1949 (Despatch No. 122)
subfiles.from: Cloyce K. Huston, Counselor of Mission, for the Acting Political Adviser
subfiles.to: The Secretary of State, Washington; divisional files
subfiles.about: Duplicates Despatch No. 122 for departmental information files.
subfiles.summary: This is an information-copy reproduction of the preceding despatch, with substantially the same text despite poorer OCR. It covers Japanese attitudes toward United States policy and national self-reliance, proposed labor-law amendments, budget drafting and taxation, and concerns that an un-Japanese activities committee might become an instrument of ideological repression.

subfiles.title: Japanese Newspaper Reactions for the Week Ending March 3, 1949 (Despatch No. 135)
subfiles.from: Cloyce K. Huston, Counselor of Mission, for the Acting Political Adviser
subfiles.about: Reviews Japanese press treatment of budget policy and Ward Price's interview with General MacArthur.
subfiles.summary: Most commentary concerned the budget and its connection to the nine-point economic stabilization program, with newspapers differing over price adjustment, administrative retrenchment, monetary policy, and the balance between stabilization and increased production. A Mainichi editorial treated MacArthur's comparison of Japan to Switzerland as the first concrete Allied statement about Japan's future role. It argued that genuine neutrality would demand national resolve, self-reliance, and acceptance of its responsibilities.

subfiles.title: Press Reactions to Ward Price's Interview with General MacArthur (Despatch No. 137)
subfiles.from: Cloyce K. Huston, Counselor of Mission, for the Acting Political Adviser
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese editorial reactions to MacArthur's statements about neutrality, defense, self-sufficiency, and Japan's political future.
subfiles.summary: Japanese newspapers drew reassurance from MacArthur's declaration that an attacked Japan would be defended, but emphasized that neutrality could not rest solely on foreign protection. Asahi, Tokyo Shimbun, Yomiuri, Hochi Shimbun, and Nichi Nichi argued that neutrality required economic self-sufficiency, political independence, pacifist conviction, and resistance to both communist and revanchist pressures. The despatch enclosed the Nippon Times version of Ward Price's interview.

subfiles.title: America Wants Japan to Be Neutral in War, MacArthur Declares
subfiles.doc_type: newspaper article enclosed with diplomatic despatch
subfiles.from: G. Ward Price, London Daily Mail correspondent
subfiles.about: Presents Ward Price's interview with General Douglas MacArthur concerning Japan's neutrality, defense, economic future, and place in Pacific strategy.
subfiles.summary: MacArthur said the United States wanted Japan to remain neutral rather than fight in another war, while assuring that Japan would be defended if attacked. He described a Pacific defense line running through the Philippines, Ryukyus, Okinawa, Japan, and Aleutians, and discounted the Soviet Union's ability to mount an amphibious assault. He also discussed Japan's prospects for economic self-support, a possible future defense force, police strength, land reform, trade unions, and the character of the Occupation.

subfiles.title: Japanese Newspaper Reactions for the Week Ending March 10, 1949 (Despatch No. 145)
subfiles.from: Cloyce K. Huston, Counselor of Mission, for the Acting Political Adviser
subfiles.about: Discusses press criticism of Ken Inukai's coalition maneuvering and reaction to Vyshinsky's replacement of Molotov.
subfiles.summary: Yomiuri, Mainichi, and Tokyo Shimbun criticized Democratic Party president Ken Inukai for trying to draw his party into a conservative coalition after the Democratic Liberal Party had won a majority. The papers portrayed Japanese parties as power-seeking factions and argued that the attempted coalition disregarded the electorate. Editorials also considered the replacement of Molotov by Vyshinsky, generally judging Soviet policy too impersonal to change greatly because of one personnel shift.

subfiles.title: Japanese Newspaper Reactions for the Week Ending March 17, 1949 (Despatch No. 167)
subfiles.from: Cloyce K. Huston, for the Acting Political Adviser
subfiles.about: Surveys editorials on selling government property, the Economic Stabilization Board's white paper, and a proposed un-Japanese activities committee.
subfiles.summary: Newspapers debated the sale of government-owned enterprises and property, questioning valuations, tax consequences, and the proposed transfer of railways and communications to private ownership. Coverage of the Economic Stabilization Board's white paper acknowledged higher real wages and signs of stabilization but stressed continued dependence on American aid, weak trade performance, and living standards still below prewar levels. Mainichi and Asahi warned that a cabinet-controlled un-Japanese activities committee might revive thought policing and suppress legitimate Communist representation.

subfiles.title: Japanese Newspaper Reactions for the Period Ending March 24, 1949 (Despatch No. 176)
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Introduces a report on Japanese press reaction to the North Atlantic Pact and continuing debate over the national budget.
subfiles.summary: The opening page states that announcement of the North Atlantic Pact was the principal foreign news event, with reactions already reported separately by telegram. Domestic coverage continued to center on drafting the national budget, which editors treated as the embodiment of a definite policy toward inflation and economic recovery. The document continues beyond this section.
